newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian coffee traders demand imports be allowed.
newsitem.headline: Indian coffee traders demand imports be allowed.

text.p: India's coffee traders, concerned that a shortage of domestic coffee is pushing prices up, on Wednesday demanded that coffee imports be allowed. "Now is the time to import. India's peak consumption season is from October to March," said Ashwin Shah, a coffee exporter.
"We should export between January and May, when production peaks, and import when there is a shortage," Shah said.

As part of economic reforms introduced in the last two years, India freed the coffee trade from five-decades-old controls, allowing domestic growers for the first time to directly market their crops to either local or foreign buyers.
The reforms replaced a system in which growers surrendered their coffee to the state-run Coffee Board.
But India's government has yet to allow imports into a country that has traditionally had a coffee surplus.
"Globalisation has to be both ways," said Ramesh Rajah, president of the Coffee Exporters' Association, urging that duty-free coffee imports be allowed.
Rajah said the higher domestic prices and a shortage of coffee for export has caused some traders to cancel export contracts, forcing them to pay penalties to foreign buyers.
Coffee Board chairman Philipose Matthai said the cancelled contracts "will affect India's credibility as a regular supplier."
Matthai said some of the exporters who cancelled contracts were selling coffee in the domestic market to profit from the high prices.
Domestic coffee prices have shot up by nearly 30 percent to 116 per kg from around 90 rupees in the last two months.
The export price is around 90 rupees.
"So even after paying a penalty, exporters can make profits by selling in the local market," Matthai said.
India's coffee exports in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) are expected to reach 180,000 tonnes, up from 168,000 tonnes in the previous year.

N.G. Ravindranath, former head of Comark, a large coffee cooperative, said there was no harm in importing coffee that has been cured, which would reduce the risk of bringing pests and diseases into the country.
But others in the industry advised caution, warning that estimates still vary on the size of the crop expected in the 1996/97 (October-September) growing season.
The Coffee Board has projected the 1996/97 crop at 219,740 tonnes but the United Planters' Association of Southern India (UPASI), representing growers, put it at around 180,000 tonnes.
"No one knows the exact figures relating to coffee. We should not do anything in haste," said N.C. Kankani, a leading grower and former UPASI president.
"Domestic prices will stabilise by January when the new crop comes into the market. Any decision to import would badly affect the local growers," Kankani said.
J.J. Rebello, chairman of the UPASI coffee committee, feels any move to import coffee would depress domestic prices and discourage growers.
Rebello said coffee growers will find it difficult to meet a government-set production target of 300,000 tonnes of coffee annually in the next five years.
